sections.title: Microbiome Signature
sections.html:
Microbiome Signature

The microbial signature of tuberculosis is read here not as a list of organisms but as a functional rearrangement of the airway and gut communities around a known pathogen, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). Use the interactive Microbiome Signature chart on this page to explore each taxon by directional level (increased or decreased) and to open the per-organism metallome panels, where iron-handling and trace-metal traits are most relevant to the host’s nutritional-immunity battlefield.

In the lower airway, the dominant pattern is enrichment of oral-origin anaerobes and facultative taxa. Sputum 16S studies consistently identify Streptococcus, Prevotella (including Prevotella melaninogenica and oral Segatella/Prevotella-clade anaerobes such as Segatella oris), Neisseria, Veillonella, Fusobacterium, Campylobacter, and Kingella as recurrent members, with several low-abundance anaerobes (e.g., Mogibacterium, Moryella, Parvimonas micra) statistically enriched in TB sputum {{cite:cheung2013}}. Cross-sectional work links stronger inverse interactions between Streptococcus and anaerobes such as Selenomonas and Fusobacterium to lower phylogenetic diversity and to radiographic disease burden in underweight cases {{cite:ticlla2021}}. This lower-airway enrichment with supraglottic, oral-type taxa is best understood as a product of microaspiration and mucosal disruption rather than a free-living lung flora: in non-TB lungs, the same Prevotella/Veillonella-rich "pneumotype" is associated with a Th17 inflammatory phenotype and a blunted alveolar-macrophage TLR4 response {{cite:segal2016}}.

A second, near-universal feature is loss of diversity. In airway samples that capture active disease, Mycobacterium can dominate the community (on the order of ~80% of reads), with a marked reduction in richness and evenness; modeling in that cohort attributed the diversity collapse chiefly to Mtb itself rather than to the host IFN-γ response {{cite:kayongo2024}}.

The gut compartment shows a complementary signature transmitted through the gut–lung axis. Short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) producers are prominent in the load-bearing taxa here—airway Megasphaera and gut butyrate/SCFA producers such as Eubacterium, alongside Alistipes—and their metabolites are plausibly immunomodulatory. Butyrate decreases Mtb-induced pro-inflammatory cytokines while raising IL-10, an effect that could blunt protective Th1/Th17 immunity {{cite:lachmandas2016}}. The decreased oral commensals on this page (Cardiobacterium hominis, Solobacterium moorei, Arachnia propionica) round out a picture of eroded commensal structure.

Two cautions are essential. First, these are associations around an established pathogen: the signature describes the ecological context of Mtb infection, not an independent cause of disease. Second, they are heavily antibiotic-confounded—many patients receive broad-spectrum agents before diagnosis, and anti-TB regimens (notably rifampicin and isoniazid) reshape both communities during treatment {{cite:alvarado2023}}. Interpret each taxon in that light.

sections.title: The Ecosystem Story
sections.html:
The Ecosystem Story

Tuberculosis is best read as an ecosystem reorganizing itself around a single, established cause. The narrative below reconstructs how the TB-associated state plausibly emerges and self-reinforces. The opening events are well established; the downstream microbiome consequences are largely hypotheses built on associations, and they are confounded by antibiotics—both are flagged as such.

1. Infection and the iron lockdown (established). Inhaled Mtb is taken up by alveolar macrophages and triggers granulomatous inflammation. Systemically, inflammation drives hepcidin, which sequesters iron in the reticuloendothelial system and suppresses absorption—a host "nutritional immunity" strategy that also produces the anemia of inflammation characteristic of TB; in a prospective cohort, inflammation overrode erythropoietic signals in setting hepcidin, and iron was well absorbed only after treatment {{cite:cercamondi2021}}. This metal-withholding remodels the chemical environment that every microbe in the niche must survive—hence the metallome panels on the Signature chart.

2. Tissue damage and microaspiration (established → plausible). Granuloma formation, hypoxia, and necrosis injure airway epithelium and impair mucociliary clearance. Damaged, mucus-laden lower airways are more readily seeded by oral-cavity organisms through microaspiration—the same mechanism that, in non-TB lungs, enriches Prevotella/Veillonella-type taxa and provokes a Th17 inflammatory tone with a blunted macrophage response {{cite:segal2016}}.

3. Enrichment and diversity collapse (association). The result is the page’s airway signature: enrichment of oral anaerobes and facultative taxa (Prevotella, Streptococcus, Megasphaera, Campylobacter, Kingella) and loss of commensal structure, with active disease often Mtb-dominated and low in diversity—a reduction driven mainly by Mtb itself {{cite:kayongo2024}}{{cite:ticlla2021}}.

4. Metabolite-driven immunomodulation (hypothesis). SCFA producers—airway Megasphaera and gut butyrate producers (Eubacterium, with taxa like Alistipes)—may tilt mucosal immunity toward tolerance. Butyrate lowers Mtb-induced pro-inflammatory cytokines and raises IL-10, which could blunt the very Th1/Th17 effector responses needed to contain Mtb {{cite:lachmandas2016}}. Through the gut–lung axis, gut dysbiosis and reduced butyrate are linked to neutrophil infiltration and T-cell anergy, and may paradoxically hamper anti-mycobacterial immunity {{cite:alvarado2023}}.

5. Antibiotics deepen the state (established mechanism, confounder). Months of rifampicin/isoniazid-based therapy near-deplete SCFA-producing taxa and can leave dysbiosis lasting roughly 1.2 years after standard treatment—longer for drug-resistant regimens {{cite:alvarado2023}}.

Feedback loops and why it matters. Inflammation → iron withholding → epithelial damage → microaspiration and diversity loss → tolerogenic SCFA signaling → weakened bacterial control → more inflammation; antibiotics then entrench the dysbiotic floor. If this self-reinforcing loop genuinely impairs immune clearance and mucosal recovery, it offers a coherent (if still hypothetical) frame for incomplete recovery and relapse, where post-treatment relapse rates are non-trivial and far higher in drug-resistant disease {{cite:alvarado2023}}.
